item.title: DDR5 costs more than a CPU, but these 4 AM4 chips are a better upgrade
item.itunes:title: DDR5 costs more than a CPU, but these 4 AM4 chips are a better upgrade
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
We're in a strange PC hardware market right now, and it feels like the market has slowly come for everything that makes a great PC. First it came for DDR5 memory, which made a platform jump from DDR4 to DDR5 nonsensically expensive, then GPUs, and then storage. The cheapest 32GB DDR5 kit was about $480 at the start of November, while a Ryzen 5 7600X is $150 at Micro Center. The memory costs more than three times as much as the processor.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

What it hasn't yet come for as hard are these great AM4 processors from AMD, which feel every bit as much of an upgrade and save you the enormous tax of replacing your motherboard and memory along with your CPU, while elevating your gaming and productivity. If you're stuck with AM4, these four are the better buy this Black Friday.

AMD Ryzen 7 5800X3D (10th Anniversary Edition)

Still the king of AM4, still keeping pace with chips that need DDR5

  • Credit: Andrey Matveev via Unsplash
  • Credit: htomari | Flickr
  • Credit: Andrey Matveev via Unsplash
  • Credit: htomari | Flickr

The legendary 8-core, 16-thread Ryzen 7 5800X3D is probably the one chip in this list that needs no introduction, and if you ask me, it is, in many ways, the most important chip AMD created. Rated at 105W with a 3.4GHz base clock, a 4.5GHz boost and 96MB of L3 cache (of which 64MB is stacked on the compute die through AMD's 3D V-Cache), it's built for gaming. With fewer trips out to system memory, DDR4's Achilles' Heel, which is its bandwidth, matters far less than it does on a regular Zen 3 chip. This chip is the pick for AM4 owners who want a gaming experience with no compromises.

Recent benchmarks from TechSpot, most notably its 13-game test, revealed that this AM4 chip matched a Ryzen 5 9600X, which is a chip that can't run without a DDR5 kit. So far, the biggest complaints surrounding the processor itself have been around the way it is priced, but that's a problem Black Friday exists to address. The cherry on the IHS is that every 10th Anniversary unit ships with a Carbice Ice Pad in the box, and that makes the deal sweeter.

AMD's Ryzen 7 5800X3D is the company's first gaming CPU with 3D V-Cache, which adds a ton of L3 cache for even better gaming performance. It's on the older AM4 platform, but is still a potent gaming chip.

Don't waste money on inflated DDR5 systems

By  Tanveer Singh

AMD Ryzen 7 5700X

8 cores, 16 threads, and zero complaints in 2026

If the 5800X3D is the chip everyone wants, the Ryzen 7 5700X is the one I'd tell most AM4 owners to buy, at least if the price for the former is not quite right. The Ryzen 7 5700X is the next best thing, with eight Zen 3 cores, 16 threads, a 3.4GHz base clock, a 4.6GHz boost, and 32MB of L3 cache packed inside a 65W TDP.

You do miss out on the stacked cache, but it packs enough cores to game and stream with Discord, a browser and a recording running in the background, and conveniently enough, its power draw means that you don't need to negotiate either your budget or your chassis for a bigger cooler if you're coming from a Ryzen 3000 series processor.

Another reason why it's such a neat upgrade for anyone coming from a Ryzen 7 3700X or Ryzen 5 3600 is that Zen 3 puts all eight cores on one shared 32MB pool of cache, cutting out the slow trips between the separate four-core clusters Zen 2 used, and adds a 19% IPC gain. If you don't get a great deal on the 5800X3D or just want to save more, this is the one to go for.

By  Tanveer Singh

AMD Ryzen 9 5900XT

Sixteen cores without the AM5 tax

Credit: Vladimir Malyutin via Unsplash.

Not everyone on AM4 will want to upgrade their chip for gaming, and to those, the Ryzen 9 5900XT is the chip I'd recommend. It packs 16 Zen 3 cores and 32 threads, a 3.3GHz base clock, a 4.8GHz boost, a solid 64MB of L3 cache and 105W TDP. Despite the name, it's the 5950X's 16-core layout at marginally lower clocks, so it holds its own in games while also chewing through rendering, compiling, and running virtual machines.

According to Tom's Hardware, it lands quite close to the 5950X, which it measured was almost 13% ahead of a Core i5-14600K in Cinebench R23's multicore test. This chip is a productivity powerhouse, and it's not asking you to re-build your PC from scratch.

AMD Ryzen 9 5900XT
See at Amazon

AMD Ryzen 5 5500F

The newest chip on AM4

Credit: Evgeniy Bezkorovayniy via unsplash

The Ryzen 5 5500F is the newest entrant here, and its September 2026 launch is the closest AMD has come to admitting that AM4 is not done yet. It arrived less than three months after AMD pitched the 5800X3D reissue as the final send-off for AM4 owners, but with the release of the 5500F, AMD sent out an unexpected budget option with six Zen 3 cores, 12 threads, a 3.0GHz base clock with 4.4GHz boost, 16MB of L3 cache and a 65W TDP.

All of that is enough to catch the interest of anyone who is on a quad-core Ryzen 3 3100 or 3300X, because they stand to gain two cores and Zen 3's IPC. And because it uses the 5600's Vermeer chiplets rather than the 5500's APU silicon, you keep PCIe 4.0 on a B550 board. It's about 8% faster than the 5500 in games according to Tom's Hardware, and with a Wraith Stealth in the box, it's a fascinating upgrade that'll set you back less than a 16GB DDR5 stick would.

If the deal doesn't seem quite right, the 5700X is an excellent all-rounder. If you've got a productivity machine, the 5900XT is the one you want, and if you're just coming from an older quad-core chip and need a cheap lift off, the 5500F can get you there.

item.title: The Xbox wireless controller is $22 off, and it's the lowest in 90 days
item.itunes:title: The Xbox wireless controller is $22 off, and it's the lowest in 90 days
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The Xbox Wireless Controller has been a reliable pick for a while, but this bundle with a 9-foot USB-C cable makes the case even stronger. Right now, the Carbon Black model is $22 off on Amazon, dropping from $64.99 to $42.99. That's the lowest price in 90 days, and it's a smart buy if you want a controller that works across console, PC, and cloud gaming without extra cables or adapters.

Xbox Wireless Controller

The controller gets high marks and can be used across a number of different products. Get it now for one of its best prices.

See at Amazon

Why this bundle is the easy pick for mixed setups

If you've been using a generic third-party pad and noticed that button prompts feel wrong in certain titles, this is the fix. Microsoft's first-party controller displays correct Xbox button layouts across the Xbox app, Steam, Epic Games Store, and EA App.

No Bluetooth pairing dance, no driver installs, no wireless adapter. Plug the included 9-foot USB-C cable into a Windows PC and start playing immediately. When you want the freedom to play from the couch, switch to wireless and the same controller handles both seamlessly.

The sculpted surfaces and refined geometry are designed around how hands actually rest during long sessions, and the hybrid D-pad plus textured grips on the triggers, bumpers, and back case keep inputs precise without needing to grip hard. Battery life is another quiet win.

Up to 40 hours of wireless play on standard AA batteries means you're not chasing a charging dock or worrying about a rechargeable pack losing capacity over time. When the batteries dip, plug in the included cable and keep playing without a pause.

The 3.5mm audio jack handles direct voice chat through any compatible headset, and the Xbox Accessories app lets you remap buttons and save profiles for different games if you want a more personalized setup.

This isn't the most exotic controller on the market, and it doesn't need to be. At $42.99 with the cable included, it's the lowest price in 90 days and a straightforward way to cover console, PC, and cloud gaming with one pad. If you've got a PC setup or an Xbox console and want a controller that just works across all of them, this is the one to grab while it's discounted.

item.title: This open-source app lets me run Xbox Game Pass games on Android, but it's far from perfect
item.itunes:title: This open-source app lets me run Xbox Game Pass games on Android, but it's far from perfect
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A few weeks ago, I stumbled across a sideloaded Android app called DroidDeck on Reddit. Since I'm always looking to get as much out of my increasingly expensive Xbox Game Pass subscription as possible, I figured it was worth checking out. The ability to play full x86 PC games locally on my Galaxy Z Fold 8 was something I couldn't resist at least trying.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Basically, DroidDeck brings Valve's Steam Big Picture interface to Android phones, including recent Snapdragon-powered devices. It runs Steam locally inside a Linux environment, using FEX to translate x86-64 instructions for ARM-based processors. Proton, Valve's Windows compatibility layer, then helps Windows games run in that environment. It also supports mobile-specific graphics drivers to help games run on Android hardware.

The process is similar for Windows PC Game Pass titles, but it adds an extra layer. DroidDeck incorporates components from Xodus, the open-source project behind Xodus Nexus, which lets Xbox PC Game Pass games run on the Steam Deck (I covered the app a few weeks ago, and it works pretty well). These components handle Xbox-specific requirements, including authentication, licensing, and game runtime compatibility, while FEX and Proton help run Windows games on Android.

DroidDeck also works with other platforms like Steam

Fex and Proton bring Xbox Game Pass to Android

While DroidDeck works with Steam, it's also compatible with the Epic Games Store, Amazon, and Battle.net, includes installation options for various emulators, and has recently added Xbox Game Pass support.

Though I haven't tried DroidDeck's Steam integration (I plan to soon), my research suggests compatibility is pretty spotty, with indie games like Hollow Knight: Silksong running far better than something like Cyberpunk 2077 (though the game reportedly runs at lower graphics settings and resolution). In this case, I'm specifically interested in testing Xbox Game Pass compatibility with a few key titles I actually want to play on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 that I think would work well with touchscreen controls (you can, of course, also use a Bluetooth controller).

After installing the DroidDeck APK from the app's GitHub page, I signed in to my Xbox account to access my Xbox Game Pass PC subscription. Next, I picked out a few titles to download: Dredge, Dirt 5, Ball X Pit, Kiln, and Yakuza: Like a Dragon.

After each game finished downloading, I clicked the Play button beside the title in DroidDeck. I was then greeted with a surprising error, asking me to enable an Android Developer Option called Disable Child Process Restrictions that limits the number of processes an app can create. I went to Settings, searched for Build Number, and tapped it seven times to enable the feature. I then went to Developer Options and scrolled down until I found Disable Child Process Restrictions.

I finally found an app that makes playing Xbox Game Pass games on Steam Deck a breeze, but it's not perfect

Xodus Nexus brings Xbox games to Linux, making it way easier to play supported titles through Proton

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: 4 easy ESP32 projects that become more useful if you own a 3D printer
item.itunes:title: 4 easy ESP32 projects that become more useful if you own a 3D printer
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Despite its cheap price tag and approachable design (compared to other microcontrollers, I mean), the ESP32 is versatile enough to serve in robotics, circuitry, and automation projects. Heck, even without extra sensors and modules, you can build a bunch of smart home projects with nothing more than a $5 ESP32 and a USB cable.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That said, this microcontroller family’s utility grows when you bring additional components to the forefront – and I’m not just talking about cheap accessories, either. If you’ve got a 3D printer in your tinkering arsenal, you can use its ability to turn STL files into tangible models to aid a handful of DIY ESP32 projects.

ESP32-powered security camera

A 3D printer is especially useful for custom doorbell security cameras

With modern AI-heavy surveillance cameras storing private home footage on cloud servers, building your own security system with local-only cameras is the way to go when you value your privacy as much as I do. In fact, I recently put together a security camera with an ESP32-CAM board, and it’s good enough to keep an eye on my attic, especially after I paired it with the likes of Home Assistant and Frigate.

But since I wanted the camera to be able to get a clear view of the entire room instead of just the doorway, I couldn’t just toss my pint-sized companion at a random shelf and call it a day. That’s when my 3D printer came in handy, as I was able to design a neat little case to mount my ESP32 on the wall. And its utility only grows if you’re planning to build a doorbell camera, as tossing a 3D-printed case into the mix can make the ESP32 and its trigger button a lot more compact and easier on the eyes.

4 ESP32 projects that need nothing more than the board and a USB cable

You don't need extra sensors just to build a couple of ESP32 projects

1
By  Ayush Pande

DIY macro pad

And even an ESP32 S3-based controller, for that matter

The ESP32-S3 is the microcontroller I recommend to newcomers instead of the base module, and its native USB is one of the main reasons why I’m so biased when it comes to this board. Besides the standard UART port that you’d typically use for serial communication and for flashing the ESP32, the ESP32-S3 has a second USB socket – one that lets it act like a regular ol’ USB I/O device once you hook it up to a PC.

I’ve even turned my ESP32-S3 combo into a multifunctional macro pad that accepts the directional input from an analog stick and uses it to run specific commands on my PC. But if I were to build a macro pad or a controller with a bunch of buttons and directional sticks, I’d have to toss a breadboard and tons of jumper cables into the mix.

But with all the extra wires lying around, I’d end up turning my computing desk into an eyesore. A 3D-printed case could accommodate all the extra components and wires for a complex macro pad, which is why I've already started tweaking different ESP32-S3 case models to match my DIY productivity tool.

Daisy-chained matrix LED displays

A 3D-printed chassis can hide the wire mess fairly well

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

Matrix LED displays can look absolutely gorgeous as smart clocks, automated light decor, and visual alert panels. Considering the sheer versatility of the ESP32 lineup, you can render pretty much anything on your matrix LED display, provided you’re willing to spend some extra time tinkering with the code.

Heck, plenty of matrix LED display modules support daisy-chaining, and as long as your ESP32 has enough firepower to handle them, you can build an entire grid that renders cool animations, icons, and even full-fledged UIs displaying sensor information. But just like a DIY macro pad, a daisy-chained matrix LED combo is bound to look clunky if you were to display it in all its cable-riddled glory. Toss in a 3D-printed case, and you can turn even the messiest matrix LED display collection into a compact desk accessory.

5 ESP32 projects a total beginner can finish in an afternoon

If you were on the fence about ESP32, these projects will get you started in no time

7
By  Tanveer Singh

Soil moisture sensor

Personally, I’d go with an ASA roll for this one

Interfacing sensor modules with the ESP32 is often the easiest (and cheapest) way to get precise metrics of your living space, especially if you’re into building trigger-action pipelines on Home Assistant. Take a soil moisture sensor, for example. Rather than buying expensive sensors that require their own proprietary apps, a cheap analog soil moisture sensor + ESP32 combo can keep tabs on the volumetric water content in your garden. With the right YAML code, you can use these readings to trigger automated watering systems.

Unfortunately, a DIY soil moisture monitoring station is one project where you absolutely need some form of protective casing, as everything besides the water sensing blade needs to be waterproofed. As long as you’ve got an enclosed 3D printer that can handle temps suited for ASA filaments, you can build a robust case for your soil moisture detection system.

A 3D printer can make even the messiest ESP32 setup look professional

I’ve been using my 3D printer to build all sorts of enclosures for my ESP32 setup, and it’s a godsend for hiding cable clutter and mounting my painstakingly-built projects to walls and desks. Leaving aside experiments involving continuous UV exposure like my soil moisture sensor, PETG works wonders for most projects. Plus, it’s cheap enough that I can build a bunch of prototypes for less than a few dollars before settling on one that best matches my needs.

item.itunes:title: Tailscale replaced the VPN, the port forwards, and the dynamic DNS I'd been searching for years
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve been using containerized services in my home lab ever since I turned an old PC into a Docker workstation, and my self-hosting antics snowballed after I encountered Proxmox. Today, I’ve got so many productivity, quality-of-life, and data archival tools up and running on my repurposed devices that I need a second stack of admin apps to ensure they work as intended.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

This includes everything from neat dashboards and monitoring agents to reverse proxies, backup services, and authentication tools. But unlike the rest of my administration stack, a third-party app remains at the center of my home lab, and it’s none other than Tailscale. After all, Tailscale’s solid remote management features served as a solid alternative to three other services I’d spent a long time trying to configure.

This is my favorite LXC on Proxmox – and it's not what you think

I daresay this LXC is more important than the rest of my VM collection

2
By  Ayush Pande

My CGNAT-afflicted network has issues with self-hosted VPN, DDNS, and port-forwarding pipelines

And the workarounds have their own caveats

One of the biggest issues I ran into early on in my home labbing journey was ensuring my services remain accessible even when I leave my tinkering cave. On paper, I could technically use port forwarding to expose individual services to the Internet. But between all the botnets and malware floating around on the Internet, port-forwarding every tool in my arsenal poses a huge security risk.

That’s where a self-hosted VPN like WireGuard/OpenVPN comes into the equation by creating an encrypted tunnel into my network – one that I can use on my laptop, phone, and other portable devices to log directly into my FOSS stack without exposing all the services individually. I could open the ports needed for this VPN on my router, and then use dynamic DNS to ensure my devices can still find the ever-changing public IP address for my VPN server.

The problem? I’ve had to work with a Carrier-Grade NAT on my current ISP, which makes it a lot harder to put this pipeline together. For the uninitiated, CGNAT puts multiple clients behind the same IPv4 address, meaning my router doesn’t have a unique public IP address. And since my home network doesn’t have its own dedicated public IP, port-forwarding wouldn’t work. Likewise, DDNS alone can't provide a path through my ISP's NAT, while a self-hosted VPN won't be able to accept inbound connections.

Using a virtual private server as a relay can help, but most platforms require me to rent their servers, and I’d rather not burden my wallet with yet another recurring subscription. Of course, there are a couple of free VPS providers that provide low-resource systems at $0 a month, but everything I’ve tried so far has required me to sign up, often with my permanent address, phone number, and a credit card number – and that’s information I’d rather not give away to some random company, especially when something like Tailscale already exists.

I couldn’t get Jellyfin remote streaming working until I found this app

Setting up Tailscale was way quicker and easier than I expected.

2
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Tailscale replaces all three services without forcing me to spend a dime

It’s a godsend for exposing FOSS tools safely outside my LAN

Rather than requiring multiple workarounds to expose my FOSS stack, Tailscale provides a peer-to-peer mesh network – one that uses encrypted WireGuard tunnels. As for my CGNAT-affected network, Tailscale uses P2P UDP connections and encrypted DERP relays to bypass its restrictions and ensure that my home lab nodes and self-hosted services are accessible on external networks.

The best part? Tailscale doesn’t cost a penny to use, as its free plan includes everything most tinkerers can ask for. Heck, Tailscale made its free plan even more generous by increasing the max number of users per tailnet to 6. Plus, it removed the cap on the number of devices you can connect to a tailnet, but truth be told, that was never a problem for my overengineered setup thanks to a certain Tailscale setting …

Tailscale packs a bunch of other QoL features, too

In a barebones Tailscale setup, you’d have to install the app on every client machine and use the online web UI to hook it up to your tailnet. When you’ve already got dozens of devices in your arsenal and are in the habit of spinning up new services like I am, manually configuring Tailscale on every machine – virtual or otherwise – can get rather tedious.

Fortunately, Tailscale supports the subnet router functionality, which provides a neat fix to this problem. Setting a node as a subnet router allows it to act as a gateway to advertise IP subnets to practically every other device in my arsenal, including printers and other gizmos that don’t support Tailscale. I’ve played with different subnet router configurations, and currently, a mere Raspberry Pi Zero (first gen, no less) board provides this functionality for my home lab.

Then there's Tailscale Funnel, which lets me expose local services to the Internet, not just my P2P tailnet. I typically use it for self-hosted services that I wish to share with friends and family without adding them to my tailnet. That said, I typically use Authentik-powered authentication to add an extra layer of security to this setup, and shut the funnel down when it's no longer needed.

Tailscale also offers the exit node facility to route all the public Internet traffic from a specific device through a local node in my tinkering cave. I often enable this feature when I need to browse the Internet on a public Wi-Fi, as it lets me route my laptop's outbound traffic through an encrypted WireGuard tunnel. Plus, it’s really handy for accessing local banking apps and other IP-restricted services that refuse to work when I’m in a different country.

Make remote access a breeze with Tailscale

I’ve been relying on Tailscale for well over a year now, and it has held up incredibly well for my remote access needs. Sure, I still have to rely on Tailscale’s coordination servers to ensure that my devices remain accessible on the tailnet. But the actual encrypted traffic travels over a P2P connection, making Tailscale secure enough that I can use it to remotely manage and (more often than not) troubleshoot my nodes.

item.title: Apple's HomeView finally makes a wall-mounted smart home dashboard worth having
item.itunes:title: Apple's HomeView finally makes a wall-mounted smart home dashboard worth having
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using an Android tablet as a wall-mounted smart home dashboard for my Home Assistant setup for years, but I'll be honest, the experience has been less than ideal. Between worrying about keeping the battery plugged in around the clock and configuring the interface to look like something I'd actually want in my living room, getting it to work well requires way more effort than it should. Nor is it exactly plug-and-play. I need third-party apps, custom launchers, and plenty of tinkering to turn an ordinary tablet into something that feels like a dedicated smart home control panel.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Having played around with the all-new, frankly long-awaited Apple HomeView for the last week, I can confirmit offers a much cleaner alternative to solve that exact same problem. The smart display is purpose-built for permanent placement, should you opt for the wall-mounted version. It has a dedicated interface for home controls, and it doesn't have a built-in battery to worry about.

But more importantly, pairing it with Home Assistant unlocks a whole new level of functionality. I've been testing it with Home Assistant's HomeKit Bridge integration, which allows me to bring practically every device from my existing smart home setup into Apple's Home app and control them directly from the wall. Add to that all the other Apple goodness, and the result is a dashboard that combines the flexibility of Home Assistant with the stunning focus on hardware design and software polish that comes with Apple hardware.

The HomeView feels like a giant Apple Watch for your smart home, but it comes with some surprising limitations

To actually take advantage of the smart home display, you need to be a very dedicated Apple device and app user.

1
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Home Assistant and HomeKit make a surprisingly good combination

I can choose exactly which devices show up on my HomeView

One of the reasons I use Home Assistant as the backbone of my smart home is that it doesn't tie me to any single smart home ecosystem. I have Philips Hue lights, Zigbee relays, Dyson fans, WiiM streamers, and plenty of other devices connected to my smart home. The downside of using Home Assistant is that the out-of-the-box interface is far from user-friendly. Nor is it designed for the living room.

That's where Home Assistant's HomeKit Bridge integration steps in. It allows me to bridge the gap between Home Assistant and Apple's Home ecosystem by translating the instructions between them. Let's be real: I'm not about to replace every one of the dozens of smart home devices in my home with HomeKit-compatible ones.

This integration exposes basically any supported Home Assistant entity as a HomeKit accessory. I can then add the bridge to Apple's Home app and access those devices just like I would any native HomeKit accessory.

The setup is exceptionally simple. Just install the HomeKit Bridge integration through Home Assistant, choose which entities you want to expose, and pair the bridge with the Home app on your iPhone. That's it. Home Assistant handles the underlying device management, and HomeKit gives you the interface.

More importantly, you can choose exactly which devices appear in HomeKit. You don't really need every sensor or automation exposed on your dashboard. In fact, you can restrict the bridge to just the devices you want to control, keeping the interface compact. I've got just under 90 different smart home devices, so being able to choose exactly which ones show up on the screen is essential.

The other big advantage is how HomeKit communicates with accessories. HomeKit is designed from the ground up for local control, which means compatible devices can communicate with smart home devices without needing internet connectivity. And while that's true for HomeKit accessories, it's equally true when working via the HomeKit Bridge. item.title: An unofficial GTA 6 PC port is making progress, and developers have the first in-game visuals to show for it
item.itunes:title: An unofficial GTA 6 PC port is making progress, and developers have the first in-game visuals to show for it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Cyberleek released the GTA 6 Xbox executable, sparking multiple unofficial PC port projects.
  • VIctory boots and renders GTA 6 on PC, but the visuals are basic, and the framerate is poor.
  • There's currently no clean way to dump Xbox Series X/S games, so porting efforts are relying on the leaked Xbox copy.

The GTA 6 PC port situation is heating up after Cyberleek released the missing executable developers need to start working with the game's leaked Xbox build. While Leonida, one of the leading GTA 6 PC ports, is dead because it got too big for its team to manage, several other projects have popped up in its place.

One of the most promising new efforts, VIctory, has managed not only to get the Xbox version of the game to boot on PC, but the project is also reportedly capable of rendering in-game graphics. The development process is reportedly being livestreamed on Discord with thousands of viewers. Clips shared on social media show off the game booting, loading menus at 30fps, and rendering some of GTA 6's early cutscenes.

The visuals still look very rudimentary, and the frame rate is nearly nonexistent, but it's still significant progress in a short period, given the executable released yesterday. The tests were reportedly performed on an AMD Radeon RX 6700 XT. It's important to note that I haven't independently verified any of these clips (including the ones featured in this story).

One advantage these projects have over PS5 GTA 6 PC port efforts is that the Xbox Series X/S and modern gaming PCs share the same x86-64 CPU architecture. That said, developers still need to address Xbox graphics functionality, memory management, and other system dependencies before the game can run properly on Windows.

According to VIctory's GitHub page, the project translates Xbox GPU shaders into DirectX Intermediate Language (DXIL) for Direct3D 12, instead of SPIR-V for Vulkan like Leonida.

There's currently no known way to dump games from up-to-date Xbox Series X/S firmware

A private GTA 6 porting project seems to be slightly farther along than VIctory

Credit: Rockstar

It's worth noting that there's currently no known way for Xbox Series X/S owners to dump games with up-to-date firmware, so all of this work is being done on Cyberleek's leaked copy of GTA 6, which is reportedly available on private torrent trackers (via VideoCardz). That raises significant legal questions, especially if developers distribute copyrighted game files or incorporate proprietary code in their projects.

In early November, Rockstar's parent company, Take-Two Interactive, targeted several unofficial GTA V iPhone, Mac, and Android ports with DMCA notices, according to TorrentFreak. Several other GTA 6 PC port projects are in the works, including CGBJ, a private build based on VIctory.

According to PortWatchVI, a website tracking the progress of unofficial GTA 6 PC ports, players can reportedly move and talk to NPCs very slowly in CGBJ, with flat-colored, mostly untextured graphics. This technically makes it further along than public projects like VIctory. Of course, like most recent porting projects, both VIctory and CGBJ are heavily AI-assisted. While PortWatchVI seems mostly vibe-coded and its percentages likely aren't an entirely accurate representation of the current status of all these projects, it's a decent estimate of how close GTA 6 is to running on PC.

In other GTA 6-related news, with PS5 Remote Play or a capture card, plus apps like Veyra and a powerful gaming PC, several people have been able to run GTA 6 at 60fps and above with DLSS 5. Though GTA 6 is now available on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, Rockstar hasn't announced a PC version.

Rumors point to an official PC release arriving somewhere between six months and a year from now, similar to GTA V. Relentless fan efforts to bring GTA 6 to PC could encourage Rockstar to release the still-unannounced PC port.

GTA 6's Xbox executable has leaked, opening the door for unofficial PC port projects to start testing

Cyberleek followed through and leaked the missing file required to get PC porting efforts underway.

item.itunes:title: 5 free Windows tools Microsoft should have built in, and the one I can't live without
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Some of the best Windows utilities are made by Microsoft, but ironically enough, most of them don't come stock with Windows. Windows 11 still can't tell you which app is holding a file hostage, bulk-rename a folder by pattern, or have a do-everything Spotlight-style search bar that's functional beyond files and apps. There are five first-party tools that belong in the OS by default, but there's also one additional third-party one that restores audio controls that Microsoft made much worse many moons ago.

Ranking the 10 best PowerToys tools you should be using

Why aren't you using PowerToys yet?

1
By  João Carrasqueira

Command Palette

One of the best parts of PowerToys

Windows Search wasn't always suboptimal, but in Windows 11 specifically, its reputation is quite poor. It has grown noisier, less trustworthy, and more confusing to use as time has gone on. To find things and perform tasks you're actually looking for, there are much better tools, and ironically enough, Microsoft makes one of the best ones.

Command Palette, the successor to PowerToys Run, is the fix. Pressing Win + Alt + Space will open it, and you can start typing immediately into a centered search box that launches apps, finds files, jumps to specific Settings pages, and does quick math without opening Calculator. There are a ton of other functions aimed at power users, and that's where it really pulls ahead of default Search. Typing > followed by a command runs it directly, so > cmd opens Command Prompt, and typing = switches to calculator mode. It can also find and install WinGet packages, which is extremely underrated.

I tried every PowerToys utility for a week, and a handful actually changed how I use Windows

While some didn't stick, others became essential tools.

By  Megan Ellis

FancyZones

A must-have for ultrawide and vertical display users

Snap Layouts is one of Windows 11's underrated additions. For halves, thirds, and quarters on a typical monitor, it's all most people need, but FancyZones is for everyone else. It's another PowerToys app where you draw your own grid of zones in its layout editor, then hold Shift while dragging a window to drop it into one.

This is a must-have for those who are on ultrawide monitors, and it's also helpful if you use a vertical display anywhere in your layout. The default snapping behavior doesn't really match how you'd actually want to split your screen up. A wide center column flanked by two narrow ones, or a portrait monitor stacked into three rows, takes a minute to build in FancyZones and stays exactly how you left it. Layouts are also saved on a per-monitor basis, so a laptop docked to an external display can keep a different arrangement on each screen.

7 PowerToys plug-ins that will change how you use your Windows PC

Take your productivity to the next level

4
By  João Carrasqueira

PowerRename

Bulk renaming made more effective

Stock Windows 11 does have bulk renaming, but it's very elementary. If you select a group of files and rename one of them, you'll apply that name to the rest of the files with a bracketed number at the end. That's about as complicated as you can get with bulk renaming by default, but PowerRename in PowerToys brings it into the 21st century.

You enter what to search for and what to replace it with, and it'll give you a preview pane that shows every original name beside its new one before anything changes. Turn on regex and it can trim, reorder, or insert text by the pattern you set. Date variables are supported too, and they let you build names like Nov-02-20-screenshot.png in one pass.

5 tools that put the Windows 11 Start menu to shame

Just forget about it

5
By  João Carrasqueira

File Locksmith

Another PowerToys must-have

"The action can't be completed because the file is open in another program" is one of Windows' least helpful and most annoying errors. It doesn't tell you what program is currently using the file, but File Locksmith actually does. It's one of the most puzzling PowerToys additions, because it really should just be in Windows by default.

If you right-click a folder or file and click "Unlock with File Locksmith", it lists every process currently using that file or folder. From there you can kill any process that's using it or expand it in more detail. Running it as admin will show you processes that are running as administrator, too.

5 Start menu alternatives and Windows tweaks that will speed up your workflow

Revamp your Windows experience with smarter Start menu alternatives and tweaks—boost efficiency, streamline navigation, and work faster

2
By  Pranav Bhardwaj

Windows File Recovery

Rescue files after you empty the Recycle Bin

Windows File Recovery is Microsoft's own undelete tool, and it's another ironic entry in this list, because it really should ship with Windows. Microsoft warns that any use of your PC after a deletion can overwrite the space the lost file occupied. Downloading and installing an app is exactly the kind of activity you'd want to avoid at that moment, so you'll need to have this installed before you need it.

It's free in the Microsoft Store and has a couple of modes: Regular and Extensive. Regular is the first thing to try for recently deleted files on an NTFS drive. Extensive will dig deeper for much older deletions or formatted and corrupted drives. It can even do FAT or exFAT media like SD cards. A command like winfr C: E: /regular /n *.docx scans C: for deleted Word documents and copies what it finds to a recovery folder on E:.

On SSDs, TRIM will likely have cleared that recently deleted thing from its flash, so recovery from solid-state is much less likely than recovery from a USB stick or hard drive, but it's absolutely worth an install.

6 utilities that solve the most annoying Windows problems

These utilities will solve common Windows problems you may be annoyed by.

5
By  Brian Burgess

EarTrumpet is what I use every day

It's not made by Microsoft, but it restores control they stifled

The tool I use every single day isn't from Microsoft, but it relies on controls that already exist on the OS thanks to them. EarTrumpet is a free, open-source volume mixer that replaces the taskbar volume popout with one that shows every playback device and every app using it. It's much more reminiscent of the volume mixer that existed in previous versions of Windows. It also lists the legacy Control Panel menus for audio controls that have since been buried in the more "modern" Settings app.

I finally became a PowerToys convert years after I should have

It took me far too long, but I finally get PowerToys now.

By  Adam Conway

These utilities all deserve a dedicated spot in the OS

It's a shame that these tools aren't included with Windows 11 by default, because most users would find them exceedingly useful, not just power users. Microsoft knows that these are gaps that exist, and that's why they create tool suites like PowerToys. Until these are included in Windows by default, do yourself a favor and install PowerToys, and if you're tired of how Windows 11 handles audio, EarTrumpet is a must-have.

item.title: I connected a tuner to my Nvidia Shield TV to record live TV to my NAS, and Plex made shows commercial-free
item.itunes:title: I connected a tuner to my Nvidia Shield TV to record live TV to my NAS, and Plex made shows commercial-free
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Since I've set up a tuner for Live TV to watch shows throughout my home, I haven't done much recording. Mainly because it requires configuring the channel guide on Jellyfin, recordings take up a lot of space, and a Plex Pass subscription is required. However, I put my hesitations aside when I learned Plex can remove commercials automatically.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That's what made me pull the trigger on a Pass subscription. Not only can I record favorite live TV shows, but I don't have to deal with commercial skipping or manual removal. Getting everything together was easier than I thought, and now live shows are available on my NAS commercial-free.

I connected an HDHomeRun to my network, and Plex took care of the rest

Adding live TV to my Shield TV Pro's server was a cinch

I put my HD antenna in a room in my house that gets the best reception. I connected it to an HDHomeRun tuner and plugged it into a Wi-Fi extender. It would be best if I could plug it straight into my router, but I used what I had because of logistics. It provides a solid connection, and I can receive live TV on all my screens.

Plex saw the tuner right away and scanned the channels. Then it created a guide, and I didn't have to ask it to. Periodically, I dial into the tuner to update it and have it scan for more live networks. The guide updates automatically, and I can schedule recordings in advance. Jellyfin, on the other hand, saw my tuner, but creating a guide and automatically removing commercials takes manual configuration.

I used Plex and Jellyfin for a month, and there's one clear winner for true hardware ownership

Your media server shouldn't need the cloud.

10
By  Jasmine Mannan

I can record while watching or schedule from the guide

Just hit the record button

Recording shows is straightforward. You can select the option from the channel guide, which is nice since you can set shows to record ahead. It works as you'd expect from a DVR, and you can also set shows to record while watching from the on-screen menu. It records the show from the moment I hit the button. It doesn't include a time-shift cache, and recording partial airings needs to be enabled.

I like the flexibility of being able to record while watching live. But the best option is using the guide so I can plan ahead for the big game or a can't-miss show. The guide provides a lineup of broadcasts for about two weeks, which is plenty of time to schedule recordings in advance. Some basic configuration and settings let me remove ad breaks and store recordings on my NAS.

I replaced my cable box with Jellyfin, and now I'm paying nothing for live TV

Paying for cable isn't necessary since I can stream live TV throughout my house with Jellyfin.

8
By  Brian Burgess

Recording commercial-free shows takes a couple of clicks

Plex removes ads and puts them on my NAS

Once I had my HD antenna and tuner connected, I created a folder on my NAS for live TV recordings. I made a new library in Plex Web and pointed it to the storage appliance. I went into DVR settings and scrolled down to select the option for Plex to detect and delete commercials. I tested it out by recording a couple of shows from the channel guide.

Plex notes that the feature can get aggressive and cut out parts of a show, especially near the end. However, I set my recordings to end a few minutes after the scheduled time for extra padding. I can also cut out other sections of a show when removing ad breaks, but I haven't noticed it on too many recordings. If something is cut in the middle of the show, it's been no more than a few seconds.

I recorded a three-hour football game, and it didn't do as well. Parts of the game were cut off, which included some big plays. Luckily, when you hit record, you can set it to detect only commercials and mark them for skipping. I've been using that option, so there's less chance of parts of the game getting cut off.

Setting Plex to detect and remove commercials takes longer than marking them for skipping. It records in real time, then processes the file afterward to remove the ad breaks. The process is also CPU-intensive, which takes extra time on my Shield TV Pro. Plex estimates it will take up to four minutes after a 30-minute show to remove them. But it varies between boxes and how much extra padding time is set.

Since it puts the commercial-free shows on my NAS, I can watch them on any screen using Plex, Jellyfin, or Emby since they all point to it. Recorded shows can use up a lot of space, depending on show length and signal quality. So, I try to be diligent about what I record and deleting what I don't want hanging around.

I connected my Shield TV Pro's Plex server to lossless CD rips, and its companion app made them portable

I finally added a NAS to my Shield TV Pro's Plex server to listen to CDs remotely with Plexamp.

1
By  Brian Burgess

Recording commercial-free live TV to storage that's accessible to all screens makes sense

I've relied on my TV tuner and servers a lot more since I canceled my streaming TV subscription. I use it during the fall since football season starts and new network TV dramas drop. It's nice to know the shows will be ad-free and stored in a central location I can access anywhere in my house. Yes, I'm paying for Plex Pass, but it's cheaper than cable or a streaming service like YouTube TV.
